text: Three hours later, they reached Haeseong. Taeo still didn't know how to tell his family everything. Nib spotted the sea gate. It never closed, Taeo said. Nib asked who kept watch.
Grandpa was waiting at the stop with a cart full of cardboard. Behind him, fishing boats sat idle under a gate zone warning.
Taeo told him he didn't have to collect cardboard anymore. Grandpa said it was fine. Nib quietly steadied the stack.
The boats were asleep, Grandpa explained, because the fish were inside the gate buoys, where nobody was allowed to go.
Sixty-four kilos of cardboard earned him 3,200 won. Taeo sent money home every month. Grandpa still pulled the cart.
Haru burst out to meet them while Grandma yelled that she'd said noon. Haru stopped in front of Nib, thrilled. The goblin was shorter than him.
Haru fired off dinosaur questions, ending with: who wins against a T. rex? Whoever sees the enemy first, Nib said. Haru objected. Nib stood by it.
Haru reminded Taeo of his last broken promise. The spicy seaweed snacks settled it. Taeo could stay.
Grandma welcomed Nib with an order to eat. Nib wiped his bare feet at the door.
Lunch was grilled mackerel. Nib took the seat facing the entrance and started boning his fish with his fingers.
He took the bones out in one piece. Grandma approved. Then he noticed the chopsticks.
He gripped one in each fist. Like knives, Haru said. Bad knives, Nib decided. Grandma let him use his hands. Grandpa and Haru joined in, and got scolded.
Then Grandma demanded the story. A gate had opened in the shop on Tuesday. Taeo had awakened as a low output summoner. Haru approved. Now Taeo could stay home.
Grandma remembered his Tuesday message. He'd only said he had eaten. He had, he pointed out. Then she used his full name.
He admitted he'd been scared, so he hadn't called. Was he hurt? When he said it was fine, she told him not to start with that.
Gates? Taeo said Nib scouted ahead, and he stayed outside. Grandpa's eyes drifted to the old family photo.
Then Taeo mentioned Kanghan's offer: fifty million won for five years with Nib. The table erupted. Haru wanted to know how many snacks that was.
Had he refused? 'Eventually,' Nib said. Grandma silently put the biggest piece of fish on Nib's plate.
But the danger remained. In twenty days, a panel would decide whether Nib was a person or a construct. A construct could be sold.
Haru said Sue the T. rex had sold for eight million dollars. Was she alive? No. Then Sue didn't get a say, Nib observed.
Grandma's ruling: Nib had boned a mackerel at her table. He was a person, and Taeo could tell the panel she said so.
After lunch, Grandpa took Nib to the breakwater. He never took anyone there. He called it the wall. Nib approved. Good wall.
Grandpa poured tea, drank first, then offered Nib the cup. On watch, they had always drunk first. Nobody had to ask.
Nib understood. Grandpa watched the sea gate. Somebody should.
He'd done three years as a coastal conscript, night watches two hours at a time. The last hour was worse than the cold. But someone always came to take over.
Nib said his own relief would find his post empty. His relief was Kett, the scout he had trained.
Grandpa looked out to sea. 'Then he'll know you didn't run.' Nib's jaw finally unclenched.
At the stop, Haru gave Nib a dinosaur sticker to match the one on Taeo's radio. Nib accepted it formally and promised to keep it dry.
Grandma packed food and told Taeo to call. Texting that he'd eaten didn't count.
Grandpa pressed his 3,200 won into Taeo's hand and closed his fingers over it.
As Taeo boarded, Grandpa straightened his backpack strap and looked toward the sea. 'Your father went in first too, you know.' Taeo froze. He had never heard that.
The doors closed before he could answer. Grandpa's smile was gone. He whispered, 'Don't you ever.'
